newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian dream team in race against financial time.
newsitem.headline: Russian dream team in race against financial time.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin has put together his most dynamic cabinet since Russian reforms began in 1992, but the dream team is in a race against time as a budget crisis eats away at the foundations of the Russian state.
The new team, spearheaded by two young first deputy prime ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, have packed ministries and the Kremlin administration with their supporters.

Since the cabinet was formed last month it has tackled some of Russia's most entrenched and politically sensitive problems, launching the restructuring of inefficient but powerful monopolies such as the gas and electricity industries, and putting pressure on persistent corporate tax debtors to pay up.
But a financial time-bomb is ticking away. Revenues have been running well below budgeted levels since last summer, prompting the IMF to freeze a $10 billion loan to Russia.

Tax receipts in the first quarter were so low -- 69 percent of budgeted levels -- that the government must present a mini-budget to the State Duma lower house of parliament next month to slash spending still further.
Trillions of roubles of wages and pensions have gone unpaid and the lack of cash threatens to choke the entire economy.
"The monstrous budget crisis is at the root of all the troubles and its size raises the question whether the state can perform its functions," Chubais told the upper house this month.
International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus is even blunter.
"The prolongation of this crisis would mean probably a major risk of anarchy and dictatorship in the country," he said.

Reforming the monopolies is not just a question of more efficiency. The monopolies are at the heart of the financial sclerosis, in which companies do not pay each other, their employees or the taxman, and the government in turn cannot pay its suppliers or public-sector wages and pensions.

Chubais, 41, a brilliant administrator who masterminded Russia's mass privatisation programme and Yeltsin's victorious re-election campaign, is one of the driving forces in the new cabinet, with overall responsibility for economic policy.
He is also one of the most unpopular politicians in Russia, a hate figure for communists and nationalists alike.
Yeltsin has balanced Chubais by bringing in Nemtsov.

Nemtsov, only 37, made his name as governor of Nizhny Novgorod, where he pioneered privatisation of small businesses and farming. His policies and youthful good looks have made him one of Russia's most popular politicians.
Described by Yeltsin as a possible successor, Nemtsov has responsibility for reforming the monopoly utilities and municipal housing, which he describes as a kamikaze mission.
The new team have quickly won the praise of the main Western governments and international agencies, who agree that vital time was lost last year during the presidential election.
"I was very impressed with the quality of the new government. It is quite refreshing to see such a strong determination to address squarely the basic issues," said the IMF's Camdessus.
Yeltsin's first pro-reform cabinet, headed by Yegor Gaidar in 1992, initially enjoyed massive public support for reforms.
But after five years in which a few have become fabulously rich while millions are poorer or face an uncertain future, there is widespread public disillusionment.

Crime and corruption put many would-be entrepreneurs off starting small businesses, while capital flight is still running at billions of dollars a year, about 10 times foreign direct investment in 1996, economists say.
Chubais, who is also finance minister, knows he must deliver the rewards of economic reform before the 2000 presidential poll -- and before the financial crisis blows the country apart.
The government is due to submit a new tax code, replacing the current unwieldy and contradictory system, to the Duma by May. The IMF has made this a condition of lending this year.
The 1997 budget requires the government to submit a sequestration, or spending cuts, bill to the Duma if revenues are less than 90 percent of planned levels in any quarter.
But the government faces a political battle royal over the cuts in the Duma, dominated by communists and their allies.

"I think it won't be impossible to get the tax code through the Duma but the sequestration issue will be really hard. And honestly speaking, it's hard for me to see right now how the Duma can agree to the kind of sequester the government is proposing," said a senior Kremlin official.
The rewards would be great.

The economy, in decline since 1989, is showing the first signs of growth this year, and could be racing ahead like an Asian tiger by the turn of the century. Inflation is heading for 12 percent this year, down from triple digits 15 months ago.
But the tax shortfall threatens all that. Either the government will allow the budget deficit to widen, which would re-ignite inflation, or it must slash spending, stifling economic recovery.
